[2025-03-11 21:53] squidwardfrommegamind : How does game score work?
[2025-03-11 21:56] stromstar : GmSc - Game Score; the formula is PTS + 0.4 * FG - 0.7 * FGA - 0.4*(FTA - FT) + 0.7 * ORB + 0.3 * DRB + STL + 0.7 * AST + 0.7 * BLK - 0.4 * PF - TOV. Game Score was created by John Hollinger to give a rough measure of a player's productivity for a single game. The scale is similar to that of points scored, (40 is an outstanding performance, 10 is an average performance, etc.). https://www.basketball-reference.com/about/glossary.html

[2025-03-24 20:49] tcm12 : When your opponent is pushing the ball in transition but then slows it down, is your defense still in transition D?  Also, on offensive rebounds or defensive fouls, it doesn't say what defense you're in (at least not in the play by play in the box score) so do you just stay in the same defense for that possession as well?  Sorry if that's unclear
[2025-03-24 20:52] spencp99 : 1) No, when your opponent slows down a fast break it reverts back to your halfcourt defense, so one of man, zone, press depending on your percentages.  2) On OREBs sometimes you will go into 2nd chance defense, which is when your opponent grabs an OREB and goes right back up with a shot. Otherwise it goes back into one of your set defenses but I haven't noticed whether it stays as the same one, same goes for defensive fouls.  You can check for yourself though by watching the live play-by-play.

[2025-04-30 00:41] fatherborf : (Invincible meme JK Simmons voice) thats the fun part, no one really knows exactly how the benefit works. is it just that the worst they can do at those skills is improved? is it functionally an actual boost to skills, and which skills? unclear exactly! additionally: is there a specific pace setting they are better at, or in a "flourish slow" situation is it always that they are better the slower it goes, so -5 is better than -2 for them? no one knows these for sure beyond "over a big enough sample they will do better matching the comment"  also important to remember there is a subtle but VERY IMPORTANT distinction between types of pace comments: 'flourish in' comments suggest a players optimal pace is slow/fast, but does not necessarily indicate they will play worse/take any sort of penalty for doing the opposite. so its an indication of where a ceiling is higher, but doesnt mean their floor gets lower in other scenarios.  'struggle in' comments are the opposite - there is no guarantee they thrive in an opposite pace, but you know they will play worse/take a penalty playing at whatever pace it says theyll struggle in. for this reason i prefer flourish comments or no pace comments > struggle in comments

[2025-05-06 23:51] naph7777 : Means that on jump shots (shots that use OS as opposed to IS or Fin) that they will shoot the same percentage from deep as they will from closer in. Which is still not particularly useful if its 20% from anywhere.  Similarly a 20 OS guy with 1 Rng, might shoot 60-70% on close in mid-range shots, but be only a 30% 3-point shooter (okay, its probably not actually that extreme and 20 OS can still hit 3's at a decent clip, but you get the idea)

[2025-05-28 16:41] _plokmijn : Stars are a rough ranking of players by current SI and POT but mean nothing except for how much of a penalty you get for RSing them. Star rating has no influence on how good a player will be. In terms of gameplay, lower stars is always better if it is a deciding factor between two players. But some people like the idea of recruiting blue chip prospects as well for their own enjoyment of the game. POT relates to their SI cap range. I forgot what naph found to be the closest but it pretty close to this: 10 = 145-155 11 = 155-170 12 = 170-185 13 = 185-200 14+ = 200+  These are just the cap ranges, many players don’t make it to that range. HS dev rate and current SI will help you determine how likely they are to reach their potential ceiling

[2025-06-01 00:49] naph7777 : Help Manual  __Scouted Skill Values vs. Real Skill Values__  So are the skill values displayed for each player accurate? Just as in real basketball, where there is some uncertainty about a player's talent level, in Hardwood there is also built-in uncertainty in displayed skill levels. The visible skill values for each player are an approximation of his current actual skill level and may deviate by up to 20% from it true value for some skills. Additionally, just like in real basketball, as a player plays more games, his displayed skill value will approach his true current skill level. Note, this may result in a player's displayed skill level actually dropping, even though he is receiving regular coaching and playing time. His skill value is not actually dropping, but because his actual skill level is better known now, a more accurate and lower value is now displayed.  __Hidden Values & Skills__  So are there hidden skills? No, there are no hidden skills. There aren't any player attributes that can be trained or improved with experience nor that erode with age. There are however fixed player values that affect certain in-game outcomes. There effect is significant, but much smaller than the affect of the relevant skill.

Then there is a player's potential for each skill which is unknown, but eluded to through the recruiting report. As a player gets more coaching and experience, his current skill level will approach his potential skill limit. Note, some skills will generally start much closer to their potential value than other skills. - Scouted Skill Values vs. Real Skill Values So are the skill values displayed for each player accurate? Just as in real basketball, where there is some uncertainty about a player's talent level, in Hardwood there is also built-in uncertainty in displayed skill levels. The visible skill values for each player are an approximation of his current actual skill level and may deviate by up to 20% from it true value for some skills. Additionally, just like in real basketball, as a player plays more games, his displayed skill value will approach his true current skill level. Note, this may result in a player's displayed skill level actually dropping, even though he is receiving regular coaching and playing time. His skill value is not actually dropping, but because his actual skill level is better known now, a more accurate and lower value is now displayed.

Heavy fatigue is something that should impact a player pretty moderately heading into the next game especially in conference tournament settings and to a slightly lesser extent (due to more time off) nationals tournament games.
